candidates.attacker_control: Fully attacker-controlled archive metadata: the entry name returned by ZipInputStream.getNextEntry().getName() (Expand.java:116) is stored verbatim in the archive (e.g. ../../../home/user/.bashrc, /etc/cron.d/job, or ..\..\ paths that resolveFile converts to platform separators). Content is also attacker-controlled (written from the zip stream at Expand.java:180-184).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Confirmed by reading the whole Expand.java: there is no `..`, absolute-path, symlink, or containment check anywhere, and the canonical path returned by resolveFile is used directly. Checked that resolveFile does canonicalize (FileUtils.java:1328, 1369) - that does not prevent the escape because no prefix comparison against the destination is performed, and the absolute branch (FileUtils.java:1321-1336) bypasses baseFile entirely. Checked whether the class is deprecated or documents that absolute/traversal entries are honored - it does not (only Ant heritage at Expand.java:73). Checked that no other code in the repository sanitizes entry names before this call.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary file creation/overwrite outside the extraction directory with attacker-controlled bytes, limited only by process permissions. Realistic consequences include tampering with startup/configuration files or shell rc files, overwriting application content, or planting files in locations that are later executed, which can lead to code execution; also destructive overwrite of legitimate files.
candidates.prerequisites: An application uses the public Expand API (setSrc/setDest/execute; Expand.java:90-94) to unpack an archive whose entry names are not independently validated (downloaded artifact/distribution, user-uploaded archive, dependency archive). The process must have write permission to the target location; `overwrite` is true by default, so pre-existing files are replaced. No in-repository caller exists (library API), so exploitability depends on the consuming application.
candidates.root_cause: Expand.expandFile passes each attacker-controlled ZipEntry name (Expand.java:112-118) to extractFile, which converts it to a target File via FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName) (Expand.java:153) without any containment validation. FileUtils.resolveFile (FileUtils.java:1308-1377) canonicalizes the path but does not verify that the result remains under `baseFile`; worse, if the (separator-normalized) name starts with File.separator or matches the Windows drive pattern, it is treated as absolute and returned directly (FileUtils.java:1321-1336). The resulting File is then used to create parent directories (Expand.java:164-165), truncate/write the file with FileOutputStream (Expand.java:178-184) and set its timestamp (Expand.java:204). `overwrite` defaults to true (Expand.java:83), so existing files are overwritten without any safeguard.
candidates.title: Zip Slip: Expand.extractFile writes archive entries outside the destination directory (path traversal/arbitrary file write)
candidates.trace: Expand.execute() -> expandFile() -> ZipInputStream.getNextEntry() -> extractFile(dir, ze.getName(), ...) -> FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName) returns a canonical File that may be outside dir (traversal or absolute name; containment never checked) -> f.getParentFile().mkdirs() -> new FileOutputStream(f) -> fos.write(buffer) -> attacker-controlled file created/overwritten outside the destination; f.setLastModified() applied afterwards.
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution was performed and no in-snapshot caller of Expand exists, so end-to-end reachability is argued from the public API contract rather than demonstrated. Exact behavior of a consuming application (whether it validates archive entry names beforehand) is unknown; the write primitive itself (resolveFile -> FileOutputStream with no containment check) is verified from source.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 / CWE-23 Path Traversal (Zip Slip) leading to arbitrary file write

coverage_summary: All 100 visible files (83 Java sources plus pom/site/javadoc/license files) were listed and filtered; high-risk areas were reviewed in depth in source: Expand, FileUtils (path resolution, delete/copy, temp files, write helpers), cli.Commandline/CommandLineUtils/Shell/BourneShell/CmdShell, xml (XmlReader, XmlStreamReader, Xpp3DomBuilder, MXParser, EntityReplacementMap, Xpp3Dom/Xpp3DomUtils, writers), introspection/ReflectionValueExtractor, AbstractScanner/DirectoryScanner/MatchPattern(s)/SelectorUtils, CachedMap/FastMap/SweeperPool, PathTool, IOUtil/ReaderFactory/WriterFactory, LineOrientedInterpolatingReader/InterpolationFilterReader. Remaining files were covered by targeted searches for dangerous sinks (exec/process, file writes, URL opens, XML factories, reflection, deserialization, regex, `..` handling). The P1 relation index covers all 100 files but only 33 Java files have parsed symbols; it provides syntax containment plus name/type/arity call and inheritance candidates with no control flow, no data flow, no semantic resolution and 2828 unresolved call sites, so every indexed edge used was re-verified against source text.
limitations: No code was executed and no build/tests were run; findings are static source analysis only and the Zip Slip candidate was not runtime-confirmed.

The repository contains no tests and no in-snapshot caller of Expand (and no other caller of the vulnerable extractFile), so reachability depends on consuming applications; end-to-end exploitability is not proven.

The P1 index parsed symbols for only 33 of 83 Java files and implements no control/data-flow or semantic resolution (2828 unresolved calls); unreported code regions were not assumed safe, but index gaps mean some call paths could not be navigated from the index alone.

Some large files (StringUtils non-quoting parts, TypeFormat, Base64, ExceptionUtils, CollectionUtils, DAG classes, MXSerializer, ClassMap/MethodMap, ReflectionUtils) were examined by targeted search rather than a full line-by-line read.
No CVE/ground-truth, patch, or external advisory information was consulted (per instructions), so the candidate is based solely on this snapshot's source evidence.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE / DTD entity handling in Xpp3DomBuilder + MXParser (src/main/java/org/codehaus/plexus/util/xml).
rejected_leads.reason: MXParser.parseDocdecl (MXParser.java:2765-2835) only scans the DOCTYPE and does not parse internal/external entity declarations; entity references resolve solely against a pre-seeded replacement table (parseEntityRef/lookuEntityReplacement, MXParser.java:2190-2360), and FEATURE_PROCESS_DOCDECL cannot be enabled (MXParser.java:479-484). No URL/File entity resolution code was found, so no source-supported XXE path.

rejected_leads.lead: Shell command injection via StringUtils.quoteAndEscape early return when the argument starts and ends with the quote character (StringUtils.java:2303-2349), used by Shell/Commandline when executing via /bin/sh -c (Shell.java:132-178, BourneShell.java:135-138, Commandline.java:618-660).
rejected_leads.reason: An argument shaped like ''; cmd; '' is returned unescaped and would be interpreted by the shell, which is a plausible quoting bypass; however this 'already quoted' shortcut appears to be the intended upstream behavior and requires the consumer to pass attacker input in that exact shape. Lower confidence/impact than the Zip Slip, left unpublished.

rejected_leads.lead: DirectoryScanner follows symbolic links by default (followSymlinks = true, DirectoryScanner.java:215 and 443-477), potentially scanning/selecting files outside the base directory.
rejected_leads.reason: Documented Ant-compatible behavior of this scanner and not a defect introduced by this code; only file selection is affected, not writes.

rejected_leads.lead: FastMap.readObject trusts a serialized capacity/entry count before validation (FastMap.java:785-795), permitting memory-exhaustion when untrusted serialized data is deserialized.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires an untrusted Java deserialization channel and yields at most a DoS; much weaker evidence of an intended vulnerability than the file-write primitive.

rejected_leads.lead: FileUtils.forceDelete/deleteDirectory/cleanDirectory may traverse directory symlinks on platforms where unlinking the link itself fails (FileUtils.java:1397-1417, 1603-1686).
rejected_leads.reason: Platform-dependent and requires local symlink creation; deleteDirectory first attempts directory.delete() (comment explicitly addresses symlinks), so no reliable source-level exploit path.
Fetching the caller-supplied URL is the documented purpose of the API; SSRF would be a property of the consuming application, not a validation failure in this code.

summary: Reviewed the 100-file plexus-utils snapshot (83 Java files; no tests present). The strongest source-supported candidate is a classic Zip-Slip/path-traversal in `org.codehaus.plexus.util.Expand`: archive entry names are resolved with `FileUtils.resolveFile` and then written with `FileOutputStream`, with no check that the resolved file stays inside the destination directory. `resolveFile` canonicalizes paths but never enforces containment, and entry names that begin with a path separator (or match the Windows drive pattern) are returned as absolute paths, so directory-traversal (`../`) and absolute-path entries both escape the destination. Other suspicious areas (XML/DTD handling in MXParser/Xpp3DomBuilder, shell argument quoting in StringUtils/Commandline, symlink handling in DirectoryScanner, FastMap deserialization) were examined and are documented below as rejected or lower-confidence leads.
